item.title: Lake Nakaumi and Yonago: Water, Birds and Sunsets — Guide
item.description: Lake Nakaumi is a vast brackish lagoon straddling the border of Tottori and Shimane, spreading beside the city of Yonago in western Tottori. Neither quite sea nor lake, its shallow waters are a haven for waterbirds — swans and countless migratory species winter here, making it one of the region’s great birdwatching spots — and its wide, open horizon delivers some of the most celebrated sunsets in the San’in region. Around it lie waterside parks, an island linked by bridge, and views across to Mount Daisen rising beyond.

item.title: Lake Nakaumi Bird Sanctuary: Winter Waterfowl by Matsue — Guide
item.description: Lake Nakaumi, the large brackish lagoon east of Matsue linked to Lake Shinji and the sea, is one of Japan’s most important wetlands for waterbirds and is registered under the Ramsar Convention. Each winter it fills with vast flocks of migrating ducks, geese and swans, alongside herons, cormorants and birds of prey, drawn to its shallow waters and surrounding reed beds and rice fields. Bird hides and observation points around the shore, including a nature centre, let visitors watch the flocks in comfort, and the winter congregations — thousands of birds rising at once — are a genuine wildlife spectacle in a region better known for shrines.

item.title: The Kako River Wetlands: Birds and Riverside Paths — Guide
item.description: The Kako River is the longest river in Hyogo, and where it widens toward the Seto Inland Sea at Kakogawa it becomes something quietly rewarding: a broad, shallow, braided channel of reed beds, gravel bars and shifting sandbanks. Herons and egrets stalk the shallows all year, and autumn and winter bring ducks, waders and other migrants down onto the open water. Level, well-surfaced paths run for kilometres along both banks, making this one of the easiest places in the prefecture for an unhurried walk or a flat cycle ride with a hire bike.

item.title: Lake Biwa's Reed Marshes: Golden Wetlands of the Lakeshore — Guide
item.description: The reed marshes of Lake Biwa are one of the lake’s quietest treasures: broad beds of yoshi reed fringe the shoreline, most beautifully around the Nishinoko lagoon near Omihachiman, where a maze of willow-lined waterways winds between the reeds. These wetlands are a designated cultural landscape, harvested each winter for traditional reed screens and thatch, and alive with herons, grebes and migrating waterfowl. The classic way to experience them is a slow flat-bottomed boat, poled or motored through the corridors of reed that filter the lake’s water and glow gold in the low light of autumn.

item.title: Tone River Wetlands: Reed Marshes on Japan's Second Longest River — Guide
item.description: The Tone River, Japan’s second-longest river, has played a vital historical role as a trade and transport artery for the Kanto region since the Edo period. Where it approaches the Pacific in Ibaraki, extensive reed marshes and wetlands line the lower river, supporting a range of birdlife and offering a quieter, more contemplative landscape than the region’s more visited attractions. The wetlands are especially atmospheric in late afternoon, when golden light catches the tall reeds along the waterway.

item.title: Mangoku-ura: A Ramsar Wetland for Migratory Birds — Guide
item.description: Mangoku-ura is a shallow coastal inlet near Ishinomaki designated as a Ramsar Wetland — twice daily the tide exposes vast tidal flats that host thousands of migratory shorebirds including dunlin, golden plover and rare spoonbill in spring and autumn. The surrounding pine forest and salt marsh ecosystem was heavily damaged in 2011 but has recovered remarkably, with bird populations now higher than pre-disaster counts. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ishinomaki, Miyagi Hours Always open; low tide for best flats viewing Admission Free Time needed About 1.
